strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Use an adaptive differential-evolution search whose population members are complete feasible sample vectors. Differential vectors combine changes across many coordinates, allowing the search to move in directions unavailable to the supplied pair-transfer descent. Binomial crossover, exact-score greedy selection, and a bounded archive provide exploration and exploitation without derivatives or an assumed convex model.

This is materially different from the supplied pairwise line search and basin hopping, and from the earlier epigraph/SLSQP, smoothed-gradient, cross-entropy, and majorization-minimization approaches. The central update here is a difference mutation between distinct feasible population members followed by coordinate crossover and one-to-one survivor selection. It does not fit a Gaussian distribution to elites, optimize an epigraph, use a smooth surrogate, or construct a convex majorizer.

The exact facts are that the evaluator uses every finite-support linear-correlation lag and that feasibility is a capped simplex. The lag objective is generally nonconvex. The heuristic hypothesis is that population-wide proposals, diverse starts, and adaptive mutation parameters may escape a local basin and find a lower exact score. Differential evolution is not a global-optimality certificate and may fail to improve the supplied construction. Preserve a validated parent as an exact-score fallback and do not claim that the target bound will be reached.

2. Mathematical specification

For n samples, represent h as a float64 vector of shape (n,), set dx=2.0/n, and require 0<=h[i]<=1 and sum_i h[i]=n/2. Then dx*sum_i h[i]=1. For each integer lag k from -(n-1) through n-1, define I_k as the integers i satisfying max(0,-k)<=i<min(n,n-k). The evaluator's lag at full-correlation index k+n-1 is

L_k(h)=dx*sum over i in I_k of h[i+k]*(1-h[i]).

The exact minimized score is C(h)=max_k L_k(h), computed in code as max(np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n)). This is finite-support linear correlation: include both lag directions and the truncated overlap at each nonzero lag. Do not use circular correlation, omit boundary terms, or substitute an autocorrelation identity. Every candidate's ranking and the returned score use this exact expression; there is no surrogate objective.

The feasible set is S={h: 0<=h[i]<=1, sum_i h[i]=n/2}. The joint Euclidean projection of a finite vector z onto S is P(z)[i]=clip(z[i]-lambda,0,1), where lambda solves sum_i clip(z[i]-lambda,0,1)=n/2. Compute lambda by monotone bisection and apply a bounded residual correction; never use clip-then-rescale.

The population has P feasible vectors x_i in R^n and exact scores C(x_i). In the exploratory phase, use the DE/rand/1 donor v=x_r1+F*(x_r2-x_r3). In the exploitation phase, use the DE/current-to-pbest/1 donor v=x_i+F*(x_pbest-x_i)+F*(x_r1-x_r2), optionally drawing x_r2 from a bounded archive of previously replaced feasible vectors. The indices r1,r2,r3 are distinct population indices, all different from target i; in the current-to-pbest phase r1 differs from i and r2 is chosen from the population-plus-archive excluding i and r1. All donor differences have zero sum when their inputs are feasible, but binomial crossover need not preserve the sum. Therefore project every crossed proposal onto S before scoring it.

For crossover, form a trial from donor v and target x_i by independently choosing donor coordinate j with probability CR, choosing the target coordinate otherwise, and forcing one uniformly selected coordinate to come from v. Accept the projected trial for that population slot only when its exact score is lower than the old slot's score by more than 1e-12. Maintain a separate global incumbent, updated only by feasible candidates with finite exact scores and the same strict-improvement rule.

3. Implementation procedure

3.1. Write one complete program defining run(seed=42, **kwargs) and all helper functions at module top level. Use NumPy and math; no external optimizer is needed. Do not use nested helper functions, closures, or lambdas. Use only sequential work on the one-CPU harness, no filesystem or network I/O, and no printed output. The pre-imported evaluate_erdos_solution may remain unused because the exact formula is specified here. Read initial_h_values at runtime; do not redefine it, serialize it, or hard-code any of its entries.

3.2. Resolve n and validate the optional parent inside run. Attempt to convert initial_h_values to a float64 NumPy array. Treat it as a dimension source only if it is one-dimensional with 1 through 999 entries; use its length as n even if its values later fail validation. If no usable parent dimension exists, accept kwargs.get('n_points') only when it is a non-boolean integer-valued scalar in [1,999]; otherwise use n=47. If a usable parent dimension exists, it takes precedence over kwargs. Do not change the supplied resolution or interpolate the parent.

A parent is eligible as a construction and fallback only if it has shape (n,), finite entries, each entry in [-1e-8,1+1e-8], and absolute mass error no greater than 1e-6. Clip only the permitted tiny bound excursions. If the clipped vector already meets the program's feasibility predicate, preserve a copy directly; otherwise pass it through project_capped. Keep a successfully validated parent-derived vector separately from the evolving population. If parent validation or projection fails, use no parent but retain n when its length was usable. Always make h_uniform=np.full(n,0.5). For n=1, return h_uniform and its in-program exact score directly, since it is the only feasible vector.

Convert seed to int and create np.random.default_rng(seed). If conversion or generator construction fails, use 42. Use this generator for every random choice so all program operations are reproducible for a fixed usable seed.

3.3. Implement top-level helpers project_capped(z,n), is_feasible(h,n), and exact_score(h,n). project_capped rejects a wrong shape, nonfinite values, or any input entry with absolute value above 1e6. For accepted z, bracket lambda with lo=min(z)-1 and hi=max(z). At lo the clipped sum is n; at hi it is zero. Perform 80 bisection iterations, setting lo=mid when sum(clip(z-mid,0,1))>n/2, and hi=mid otherwise. Set h=clip(z-(lo+hi)/2,0,1).

Correct any remaining residual r=n/2-sum(h) deterministically in increasing coordinate order. If r>0, add no more than 1-h[i] at each coordinate and subtract the addition from r. If r<0, subtract no more than h[i] and add the subtraction to r. Recompute the residual after the pass and make another bounded correction if necessary. Return None if h is nonfinite, any entry is outside [0,1], or the final absolute mass error exceeds 1e-9. Do not rescale. is_feasible requires shape (n,), finite values, strict bounds 0<=h[i]<=1, and absolute mass error at most 1e-8.

exact_score first requires is_feasible. Compute corr=np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n), require shape (2*n-1,) and finite entries, and return float(np.max(corr)). Return positive infinity on any failed check. This direct score is authoritative for the population, start pool, incumbent, fallbacks, and final return.

3.4. Implement a top-level candidate-adder that receives a pool, proposed vector, family label, and n. If the proposal is already feasible, copy it; otherwise call project_capped. Reject failed projections, infeasible vectors, nonfinite exact scores, and duplicates whose maximum absolute coordinate difference from a pool member is below 1e-8. Store a copy, its exact score, and its family label. Do not let later mutation of an array alter a stored candidate.

Build the initial pool algorithmically. Add uniform first and a valid parent directly. If a parent exists, also propose its reversal, complement 1-parent, and complemented reversal as diversity starts. Add a block vector with floor(n/2) leading ones, a 0.5 next entry when n is odd, and zeros elsewhere; an alternating zero/one vector; and a seeded balanced binary vector made by permuting indices, assigning floor(n/2) ones, and assigning one 0.5 entry when n is odd. Add profiles 0.5+0.45*cos(2*pi*m*arange(n)/n+phase) for m=1,2,3 and phases 0 and pi/2. Project every proposal even if its construction appears feasible.

Add Gaussian perturbations at standard deviations 0.025, 0.06, 0.14, and 0.30 around the valid parent when present and around uniform. Add one seeded uniform-[0,1] vector. Give these candidates family labels such as parent, uniform, symmetry, binary, wave, noise, and random. If the pool has fewer than 2P distinct vectors, make further projected Gaussian proposals around the parent or uniform, using the four noise scales cyclically and alternating the center when both are available. Make at most 12P further attempts. Score every stored candidate exactly.

3.5. Select the P-member initial population from the scored pool. Include the parent and uniform candidates first when present and distinct. Then include the lowest-score unused candidate from each available family in the fixed order symmetry, binary, wave, noise, random, until reaching P. Next add candidates in increasing exact-score order until at least max(current population size, ceil(P/3)) members are selected. Fill remaining slots with farthest-point selection: for each unused candidate compute its minimum root-mean-square coordinate distance to any selected member, choose the candidate with the largest such distance, and break exact distance ties by lower exact score and then lower pool index. If fewer than P distinct pool members exist after the bounded generation attempts, fill remaining slots with copies of valid selected candidates; population indices remain distinct even if their vector values coincide.

Initialize the global incumbent by exact-scoring uniform and the validated parent, then compare every candidate in the full start pool, not only selected population members. Store the best vector as an independent copy. This makes a good start that was not selected for population diversity eligible for return.

3.6. Implement a top-level differential-evolution helper receiving the population and scores, n, the generation and stall caps, restart cap, start pool, RNG, and the current global incumbent. Keep population vectors feasible at all times. The generation count includes any generations after population restarts; never exceed the configured cap.

At the start of each generation, copy the population and scores to old-generation arrays. Sort indices deterministically by the tuple (exact score, index); use that order for p-best selection. Use the DE/rand/1 donor for the first ceil(0.25*max_generations) generations. For each target i, draw r1,r2,r3 uniformly without replacement from population indices other than i and form v=x[r1]+F_i*(x[r2]-x[r3]). For later generations, let p_count=max(2,ceil(0.2*P)), choose pbest uniformly among the p_count lowest-scoring members, excluding i when another top member is available, draw r1 from the population excluding i, then draw r2 uniformly from the union of population entries excluding i and r1 and archive entries. Form v=x[i]+F_i*(x[pbest]-x[i])+F_i*(x[r1]-x[r2]). Use only old-generation population vectors during a generation; newly accepted vectors become available in the next generation.

Use success-adaptive mutation parameters. Initialize mu_F=0.55 and mu_CR=0.85. For each target, sample F_i from a Cauchy distribution with location mu_F and scale 0.1, retrying nonpositive or nonfinite draws at most 10 times; if all retries fail, use mu_F. Clip the usable F_i to [0.05,1]. Sample CR_i from a normal distribution with mean mu_CR and standard deviation 0.1, then clip to [0,1]. Form binomial crossover from v and old x[i] using CR_i and force one random donor coordinate. Reject nonfinite donor or trial arrays. Project the crossed vector with project_capped and compute exact_score only if it passes is_feasible.

Accept a trial into slot i only if its exact score is less than old_scores[i]-1e-12. In that case write the trial and score into the next-generation arrays, append a copy of the displaced old x[i] to a next-archive list, and record F_i and CR_i as successful parameters. Otherwise copy the old member into the next generation. Independently compare every feasible finite trial with the global incumbent using the same 1e-12 strict-improvement threshold.

After processing all targets, install the next-generation population. Make the archive consist of the prior archive plus displaced vectors, and if it exceeds P entries remove uniformly random entries until its length is at most P. When at least one trial was accepted, update the parameter memories with c=0.1: mu_F=(1-c)*mu_F+c*(sum(F_success^2)/sum(F_success)) and mu_CR=(1-c)*mu_CR+c*mean(CR_success). Clip mu_F to [0.05,1] and mu_CR to [0,1]. If no trial was accepted, leave both memories unchanged.

3.7. Track stagnation against the global exact incumbent. Save its score at the start of each generation; reset the stall count if it improves by more than 1e-12 during that generation, otherwise increment the count. When the count reaches the size-dependent stall limit and a restart remains, restart the population if another generation is available. Sort the current population by exact score and retain its best ceil(P/2) members. Ensure the global incumbent is among the retained members; if absent, replace the worst retained member with a copy and stored exact score of the incumbent. Refill the other slots using projected Gaussian perturbations of the global incumbent with restart standard deviation cycling through 0.04, 0.12, and 0.25. For each slot, make at most five attempts, multiplying the scale by 1.5 after a duplicate or failed projection and capping it at 0.5. If attempts fail, use the farthest unused start-pool member from the retained vectors; if none exists, use a copy of a retained feasible member. Exact-score each refill candidate. Clear the archive, reset mu_F and mu_CR to their initial values, reset the stall count, and increment the restart count. If the stall limit is reached after all permitted restarts, terminate early. Otherwise terminate only at the generation cap or a specified numerical failure that prevents further population updates.

A restart does not remove or alter the separately stored global incumbent, parent fallback, or uniform fallback. A branch or candidate with invalid numerical values is discarded; it must not abort valid remaining work. Catch exceptions around an individual generation or restart where possible, preserving the last valid population and incumbent. If a search helper fails, continue to final selection with valid candidates already stored.

3.8. In run, choose the following size-dependent settings, build the pool and population, and call the bounded differential-evolution helper once: for 2<=n<=64 use P=64, max_generations=100, stall_limit=18, and at most 2 restarts; for 65<=n<=128 use P=48, 70 generations, stall_limit=14, and at most 2 restarts; for 129<=n<=256 use P=32, 40 generations, stall_limit=10, and at most 1 restart; for 257<=n<=512 use P=20, 20 generations, stall_limit=7, and at most 1 restart; for 513<=n<=999 use P=12, 12 generations, stall_limit=5, and at most 1 restart. All random operations and result-dependent parameter updates occur inside the generated program.

3.9. Before returning, recheck the saved incumbent, parent, and uniform fallback. Project a saved candidate again only if it is not already feasible; require feasibility and recompute its exact score. Select the valid candidate with the lowest recomputed exact score. If any optimization operation fails, retain the best valid candidate already stored. Uniform is always available. Return a one-dimensional float64 NumPy array, its recomputed Python float exact score, and Python int(n), in that order.

4. Search choices and useful variations

Use the defaults in section 3 without preliminary tuning. The remaining default settings are 80 projection bisections, 1e-8 mass-feasibility tolerance, 1e-9 projection residual tolerance, 1e-8 duplicate threshold, 1e-12 strict score-improvement threshold, p-best fraction 0.2, archive capacity P, Cauchy scale 0.1, normal CR scale 0.1, and success-memory rate c=0.1. Use the first-quarter rand/1 phase and current-to-pbest/1 phase thereafter. The initial noise scales are 0.025, 0.06, 0.14, and 0.30; restart scales are 0.04, 0.12, and 0.25.

The correctness requirements are the full finite-support lag objective, exact-score ranking and acceptance, joint capped-simplex feasibility, a valid parent fallback when supplied, and a valid uniform fallback. Population sizes, generations, crossover, mutation, start diversity, and restarts are heuristics. A coder may choose a first-phase fraction from 0.2 to 0.35, p-best fraction from 0.1 to 0.3, mu_F initially from 0.4 to 0.7, mu_CR from 0.7 to 0.95, and nearby perturbation scales from 0.02 to 0.35. A coder may modestly reduce size-dependent population or generation counts, but must keep finite hard caps and enough population members for distinct donor indices. Any result-dependent adaptation must use explicit in-program rules such as the success-memory and stagnation updates above. Do not select candidates using a surrogate or claim a target score in advance.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Use float64 for every vector, population, score, and projection. Check finiteness at input, projection, mutation, candidate, and correlation boundaries. Reject a projection input with wrong dimensions or extreme magnitude. The bisection projection is monotone; its final bounded residual correction is the only mass repair. Do not repair by clipping and rescaling. Check that every stored population member, archive member, incumbent, and return candidate satisfies the box and mass predicates. Catch invalid Cauchy draws, solver-independent numerical exceptions, and nonfinite correlation results by discarding the affected candidate or ending only that search branch. Differential evolution uses no external solver, and no solver status or surrogate value is involved.

Storage is O(P*n) for the population, O(P*n) for the archive, and at most about O(2P*n) for the start pool; no dense lag-by-coordinate Jacobian, pair matrix, or cubic tensor is constructed. The exact correlation output has 2n-1 entries. Each exact score takes O(n^2) arithmetic with np.correlate, and each projection takes O(80n) work. The size-dependent limits bound single-CPU work; the largest default population-generation product is 6400 at n<=64, while budgets shrink as n grows. The n<=999 cap prevents unbounded allocation. If optimization has no valid improvement, return the best validated parent or the uniform vector rather than an unchecked proposal. Terminate by the fixed generation cap, the stated stagnation and restart rules, or a numerical failure that leaves no safe update; none is a global-optimality certificate.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

The generated run function itself must parse seed and kwargs, inspect the optional initial_h_values global, derive n, validate and jointly repair the parent when appropriate, create the seeded RNG, generate the population, execute the bounded search, test every candidate, and select fallbacks. A vector may be scored only after checking shape (n,), finiteness, strict bounds 0<=h[i]<=1, and mass error within the stated tolerance. Compute the authoritative scalar in the program as max(np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n)); reject a correlation with the wrong length or nonfinite values. Do not substitute a claim, hard-coded score, smoothed objective, or solver result.

Retain a validated parent-derived vector throughout the search and compare it by exact score at final selection. Always retain h_uniform=np.full(n,0.5). Recompute the chosen vector's exact score immediately before return and ensure the scalar matches that exact returned array. If parent parsing, start construction, mutation, projection, or search fails, continue with the best valid candidate already stored; if no search candidate survives, return the best valid fallback, using uniform when no parent is valid. Return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values a one-dimensional float64 NumPy array, c5_bound a Python float, and n_points a Python int. The program must not print results or claim that it has executed, measured, or verified an improvement.
